prime.problem: When a run goes wrong, "the agent hallucinated" is true in the least useful way. Without naming which part of the system owned the moment that failed, you can't tell a lost exit code from a bad model, so you fix the wrong thing.
prime.fits: First card of the Agent Stack series. You already know the agent loop (call, tool, append, repeat); this card puts that loop inside the ten layers around it and gives every later course its address on the map.
expect: the ten layers of the agent stack v1
ownership: run, working set, capability, side effect, evidence
the request path wrapped by trust and operator layers
approvals where side effects become real
the Tuesday run walked layer by layer
prime.goal: Take any moment of an agent run and name the layer that owns it, then use that to say where a failure really happened and which moments no layer owns.

attend: Why does the picture wrap the request path with trust and operator layers instead of stacking ten boxes in a tower?
At step 7 of the Tuesday run, which layer lost the exit code, and which layer still has it?
Where does the tool layer stop and the execution surface start when the model asks to run pytest?
Which moment of the Tuesday run has no owner on the request path, and which layer catches it afterward?
What does he give up by covering execution surfaces and identity together in Part 7?

must: One word ("agent") covers state, orchestration, capability, execution and evidence → every failure gets the same vague label → split by what each part owns → a failure becomes "which layer resolved, assembled, exposed, approved or recorded the wrong thing?"

The model only turns a prepared request into output → what it sees is chosen by the context layer and what it can do is set by tools and execution → a wrong final claim can come from a working set that lost a fact (step 7), not from the model

A tool tells the model what it may ask for, while the execution surface decides what actually happens → exposing a tool is not granting authority → approvals belong where a side effect becomes real, owned by the identity and policy layer

The request path ends at delivery, and nothing on it re-checks the final claim against the world → that check has to come from the operator loop (trace, then an evaluation such as re-running the tests) → evidence is a separate layer, not a by-product
elevated: Transcript (durable record, kept with the run) vs working set (assembled per turn) → compaction can drop a fact from the working set while the transcript still holds it → forensics can recover what the model no longer sees
reference: the exact order and numbering of the ten layers
which Agent Stack part covers which layer
the vendor examples he names (OpenAI Responses API, MCP, LangGraph, Playwright, Temporal)
the Tuesday run's specific numbers (1 failed, 41 passed)

compress.prompt: Card closed: draw the picture from memory (request path, the band above it, the column on its right, the floor below), label each box with what it owns, then place the Tuesday run's steps 6, 7 and 9 and the checker on it.
checklist: request path: interface → control plane → runtime → (context feeds) model → tools → execution
identity, policy and approvals wrap the path, with approval at the side effect
the operator loop receives evidence and owns it afterward; infrastructure underneath, its limits flow up
step 6 = execution surface (exit 1), step 7 = context layer (working set loses it), step 9 = model + interface (unchecked claim), checker = operator loop
the main idea is ownership, not the list

retrieve.q: Explain to a teammate why "which layer owns this?" is a better first question in an incident review than "what did the agent do wrong?".
answer: "agent" bundles session, context, capability, execution and evidence, which fail differently
naming the owning layer points at a specific fix (summary rules, tool exposure, approval placement, missing trace)
it also shows moments no layer owns, which is itself a finding

retrieve.q: Walk the Tuesday run from step 6 to the final message: for each step, say which layer acts, what it holds, and where the fact "exit code 1" exists afterward.
answer: step 6: execution surface runs pytest, exit 1 enters the transcript
step 7: context layer compacts; the working set now says "tests passing"; the transcript (control plane) still has exit 1
step 9: model writes "all tests pass" from its working set; the interface delivers it
checker: operator loop re-runs pytest, exit 1 again, and the trace shows where it was lost

retrieve.q: Your harness exposes a run_shell tool. A reviewer asks for an approval prompt on every tool call. Where would you put approvals instead, and what still has to stop a dangerous command once approved?
answer: approve where a side effect becomes real (push, write outside the repo), not on every call, or users learn to click yes
approval decides whether to proceed; it doesn't limit what the action can do
a sandbox or scoped execution surface still bounds the blast radius (see approval is not containment)

retrieve.q: A provider API bundles stateful continuation, tools, hosted execution and tracing. Does buying it remove layers from your map? What changes for you?
answer: no: packaging collapses faster than architecture, the layers still exist
you no longer own some of them, so you must find out where state, side effects and evidence live
failures still need a layer name, even if the answer is "inside the vendor"

compare.q: The agent-loop card has two parts, a harness and a model. Which of the ten layers did "the harness" quietly contain, and what goes wrong if you keep thinking of them as one thing?
answer: the harness held control plane (session, transcript), runtime (steps, budgets), context assembly, tool exposure and often execution
lumping them hides where state lives and who authorizes side effects
orchestration failures (retries, stale context, duplicate effects) get misread as model quality

compare.q: Measuring an agent graded outcomes with hidden tests. In the ten-layer map, which layer does that belong to, and what is the difference between the trace and the grade?
answer: both sit in layer 9, the operator loop
the trace (observability) says what happened; the grade (evaluation) says whether it was good enough
you can replay a trace forever and still have no release decision without explicit criteria

predict.q: Suppose the harness had kept the raw pytest exit code outside the working set and checked it before letting step 9's message out. Which layer would now own the check, and does the false claim still reach the user?
predict.answer: The check moves onto the request path: the runtime (or a policy gate before delivery) compares the claim with the recorded exit code, which was never lost from the transcript. The false claim is blocked or rewritten before the interface delivers it. The operator loop still matters, but now it confirms rather than discovers. Expect the done-chain card to formalize this as checking each link: request, tool, command, effect, delivered.

apply.task: Take one transcript of your own (a mini-swe-agent run viewed in trajviz, or a Claude Code session). List every event in order and tag each with the one layer that owns it, using the ten-layer table. Then mark any event no layer checked: a claim, a summary, or a tool result that was taken on trust.
apply.done: Every event has exactly one layer tag, at least eight of the ten layers appear or you can say why they are absent, and you name at least one unowned check with the layer you would give it.
apply.hint: Compaction or summarization events, and the final message, are where unowned claims usually hide. Look for the last real exit code before the final message.
